newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Belgian OLOs see gains fade away, support not far.
newsitem.headline: Belgian OLOs see gains fade away, support not far.

text.p: Belgian bond futures pared their earlier gains in the course of Monday and cash bond yields rose as the market consolidated after a stint of strong gains in line with Bunds and Treasuries, dealers said.

But prices were well underpinned. "There is quite a lot of liquidity around still...for these players it is a question of how long they want to stay in cash and miss out on a couple of points of extra yield," said one.
The presence of uncommitted cash and bottom pickers meant the downside was capped, dealers said, but it would take fresh positive news to push market yields significantly lower.

September OLO futures were almost unchanged at 118.31, slipping from an early high of 118.50. The yield on the benchmark 10-year cash OLO rose to 6.40 percent after having held steady at 6.36 percent for most of the session.

But the benchmark's spread over a similar Bund only widened by a basis point in the course of the day to 22 after having started at 21, up two from Friday. The slight widening meant OLOs underperformed Bunds only marginally.
Dealers said they would now be looking at U.S. data due later this week for trends. One noted most of the figures due were seen as 'second-tier.'

U.S. capacity use data, due at 1315 GMT on Tuesday, are forecast to show a slight increase in utilisation, while industrial output, due at the same time, is expected to have risen as well. Both are for August.
In view of a bunch of recent indicators pointing to U.S. economic strength, dealers said, Tuesday's figures would have to be much above the forecasts to upset the market.

There was more interest in news on the OLOs to be offered at next Monday's monthly auction amid talk of a new 10-year benchmark. One trader expected the issue to have a March 15 coupon date, a coupon of 6-1/4 percent and a price above par.

Longer-term, the OLO/Bund spread looked set to move in amid buying sentiment, dealers said. OLOs are expected to be propped up by the view that key interest rates will hold steady for now and that Belgium will be in the first group of countries forming an economic and monetary union in Europe by 1999.
While some traders are setting a target of 17 basis points for the differential, others foresee levels below that.

For OLOs the downside was limited since domestic accounts -- the main holders of OLOs -- would not sell to take profits, they said. Bunds did not have such a cork to float on. Some traders said this too made fresh spread gains for OLOs possible.
Domestic accounts typically hold OLOs for longer-term investment purposes rather than for trading gains.

On EMU, Belgian traders are generally confident the government will be able to slash the budget deficit to the level required in the Maastricht Treaty, thus boosting Belgium's chances to join the single currency.

Little news has emerged on the current negotiations on the 1997 budget, but traders said Prime Minister Jean-Luc Dehaene's unbending commitment to EMU meant he would ensure the necessary austerity measures -- estimated at just over 100 billion Belgian francs -- would be taken without fail.
In the run-up to EMU the spread between the countries expected to join is set to narrow.
The OLO/Bund yield differential has come in steadily from the 66 basis point level seen at the end of 1995.

One trader was sceptical about the downside scope for the spread, citing talk about a softening of EMU criteria to ensure a large number of countries could take part, which could trigger currency market swings which would also hit the franc.
He also noted that although the Belgian budget talks were progressing there was no deal yet.
-- Nieck Ammerlaan, Brussels Newsroom +32 2 287 6816
